brands: Chorionic Gonadotropin for Injection, USP (Fresenius Kabi)

usedFor: Low testosterone from pituitary deficiency in males (selected cases)

statusDetail.healthCanada: Marketed: Pregnyl 10,000 unit vial (DIN 02182904, Organon; marketed since 1997-08-13); Chorionic Gonadotropin for Injection, USP 10,000 unit vial (DIN 02247459, Fresenius Kabi; original market date 2004-09-13); Ovidrel 250 mcg/0.5 mL (DIN 02371588 marketed since 2013-05-28; DIN 02262088 also listed as marketed since 2004-12-20). Novarel: no Drug Product Database record found.
statusDetail.fda: Not re-verified in this Canada-focused pass. See openQuestions.

indications: Pregnyl (women): induction of ovulation and pregnancy in the anovulatory, infertile woman whose anovulation is secondary (not primary ovarian failure) and who has been pretreated with FSH-containing preparations
Pregnyl (men): prepubertal cryptorchidism not due to anatomical obstruction; selected cases of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (secondary to a pituitary deficiency) in males

Chorionic Gonadotropin for Injection, USP (Fresenius Kabi), as listed in its monograph. Male: prepubertal cryptorchidism (not due to anatomical obstruction), delayed adolescence, dwarfism (pituitary), hypogonadotropic eunuchoidism, selected cases of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism in males. Female: ovulation induction, abortion (habitual), infrequent scanty bleeding (functional), functional sterility
Ovidrel: induction of ovulation and pregnancy in patients undergoing fertility treatment whose infertility is functional and not due to primary ovarian failure
Other uses in men (for example alongside testosterone, or for fertility outside the listed hypogonadotropic hypogonadism indication) are not among the indications in the Canadian monographs

Not for weight loss: the Pregnyl and Fresenius Kabi monographs state hCG has not been shown to be effective adjunctive therapy for obesity and should not be used for body weight reduction. The Ovidrel monograph has no such statement
mechanism: Acts like pituitary LH: stimulates androgen (testosterone) production in the testes and progesterone production in the ovaries; triggers final follicle maturation and ovulation.

strengths: 10,000 USP units per vial (powder for solution, kit)
products.device: Multi-dose vial of powder plus a 10 mL solvent vial (water for injection with 0.9% benzyl alcohol and 0.56% sodium chloride); intramuscular use only

products.brand: Chorionic Gonadotropin for Injection, USP (Fresenius Kabi)
products.device: Vial of powder plus 10 mL multiple-dose vial of bacteriostatic water for injection with 0.9% benzyl alcohol; intramuscular or subcutaneous
Ready-to-use pre-filled syringe or pre-filled pen (pen supplied with 2 needles); single use; subcutaneous

strengths: Solution (strength for this DIN not retrieved)

deviceNotes: Pregnyl: reconstitute by adding 1 to 10 mL of the solvent to the powder and agitating gently until dissolved; with 10 mL the concentration is 1,000 USP units/mL
Fresenius Kabi: add up to 10 mL of the supplied bacteriostatic water and mix gently until reconstitution is complete
Ovidrel pre-filled syringe is for a single subcutaneous injection; Ovidrel pen and needle are used once, then the pen is discarded

doseInfo.regimen: 5,000 to 10,000 USP units intramuscularly one day following the last day of treatment with an FSH-containing preparation (the monograph notes 10,000 USP units is the dose recommended in FSH product labelling)
doseInfo.maxDose: 10,000 USP units (top of the listed range)

doseInfo.population: Prepubertal boys, cryptorchidism not due to anatomical obstruction (Pregnyl)
doseInfo.regimen: 4,000 USP units 3 times weekly for 2 to 3 weeks, or 1,000 USP units 3 times weekly for 6 to 8 weeks
doseInfo.maxDose: 4,000 USP units per injection as listed
doseInfo.durationOrContext: The monograph states the average appropriate age appears to be 12 years

doseInfo.regimen: 4,000 to 5,000 USP units 3 times weekly for 6 to 8 weeks, with a rest period of 2 to 3 weeks between courses
doseInfo.maxDose: 5,000 USP units per injection as listed
doseInfo.durationOrContext: Courses separated by 2 to 3 week rests

doseInfo.regimen: 4000 USP units three times weekly for two to three weeks, or 1000 USP units three times weekly for six to eight weeks
doseInfo.maxDose: 4000 USP units per injection as listed

doseInfo.population: Men, hypogonadism after sexual maturity (Fresenius Kabi)
doseInfo.regimen: 4000 to 5000 USP units three times weekly for six to eight weeks, with a rest period of two to three weeks between courses
doseInfo.maxDose: 5000 USP units per injection as listed
doseInfo.durationOrContext: Monograph lists this under 'Hypogonadism (after sexual maturity)'

doseInfo.regimen: 5000 to 10 000 USP units one day following the last dose of gonadotropins
doseInfo.maxDose: 10 000 USP units (top of the listed range)
doseInfo.durationOrContext: Gonadotropin dosing per that product's own prescribing information

doseInfo.regimen: 250 mcg subcutaneously one day following the last dose of the follicle stimulating agent, once adequate follicular development is shown by serum estradiol and/or vaginal ultrasound
doseInfo.maxDose: 250 mcg single dose (no maximum otherwise stated)
doseInfo.durationOrContext: Withheld if there is an excessive ovarian response (multiple follicles, significant ovarian enlargement or excessive estradiol)

missedDose.text: Not stated in the fetched monograph text.

storage.unopened: Pregnyl: 15 to 30 C. Fresenius Kabi: controlled room temperature (below 25 C) until expiry. Ovidrel: 2 to 8 C (refrigerator), do not freeze, keep in original package, protect from light; the pre-filled syringe (not the pen) may be kept at 25 C for up to 30 days, then discarded
storage.inUse: Pregnyl reconstituted: stable 28 days refrigerated (2 to 8 C). Fresenius Kabi reconstituted: keep refrigerated (2 to 8 C) and use within 30 days. Ovidrel: single use; discard any unused material

byProduct.brand: Chorionic Gonadotropin for Injection, USP (Fresenius Kabi)

commonSideEffects: Pregnyl: headache, irritability, restlessness, depression, fatigue, edema, precocious puberty, gynecomastia, injection-site pain, allergic reactions
Ovidrel: injection-site pain 16.2% (ovulation induction study); application site disorders 14.6%
Ovidrel: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, headache and mild or moderate OHSS listed as common (more than 1 in 100)
warnings: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) can be triggered by hCG; patients are followed for at least two weeks after hCG. Ovidrel monograph: maximum severity at 7 to 10 days; patient leaflet gives incidence usually under 3%; independent risk factors include age under 30 and lean body mass
Multiple pregnancy: increased risk with ovulation induction (Ovidrel trial: 2 of 15 live deliveries, 13.3%, were multiple births)
Thromboembolic events reported both with and separate from OHSS (Pregnyl); Ovidrel lists thromboembolism as very rare (1/10,000)
Ectopic pregnancy, pregnancy loss and possibly congenital malformations are more frequent with assisted reproduction; ovarian torsion reported after hCG
Prepubertal boys: use cautiously to avoid premature epiphyseal closure or precocious sexual development
Men: hCG increases androgen production
Heart or kidney disease, epilepsy, migraine or asthma (or a history of them): close supervision, as aggravation or recurrence may occur
Pregnancy tests: hCG may interfere for up to ten days with serum/urinary hCG tests
Not for weight loss: Pregnyl and Fresenius Kabi monographs state hCG has not been shown effective for obesity and should not be used for body weight reduction
Male uses outside the listed indications are not in the Canadian monographs
contraindications: Pregnyl: prepubertal boys with signs of anatomical obstruction; precocious puberty; hypersensitivity; known or suspected sex hormone-dependent tumours (ovary, breast, uterine carcinoma in females; prostatic or breast carcinoma in males); reproductive organ malformations or uterine fibroids incompatible with pregnancy; abnormal (non-menstrual) vaginal bleeding of unknown cause

Fresenius Kabi adds: pituitary tumour, ovarian tumour, androgen-dependent neoplasms; uncontrolled endocrine disorders (e.g. hyperprolactinemia, thyroid and adrenal dysfunction); primary ovarian failure; active thrombophlebitis or thromboembolic event; allergy to u-hCG

Ovidrel: hypersensitivity; primary ovarian failure; uncontrolled thyroid or adrenal dysfunction; hypothalamic or pituitary tumours; abnormal uterine bleeding of undetermined origin; ovarian enlargement or cyst of unknown cause; ovarian, uterine or mammary cancer; pregnancy
interactions: Pregnyl: interactions not studied; interactions with commonly used medicines cannot be excluded
Ovidrel: no clinically significant drug interactions reported during hCG therapy
Interferes with hCG pregnancy tests for up to ten days
specialPopulations: Pregnancy: Pregnyl not used after pregnancy is established; Ovidrel contraindicated in pregnancy
Breastfeeding: Pregnyl must not be used during lactation; Ovidrel not indicated during breastfeeding
Children: Pregnyl and Fresenius Kabi list prepubertal cryptorchidism; Ovidrel is only for female patients of reproductive age
wada: Chorionic gonadotrophin (CG) is prohibited at all times in males (2026 Prohibited List, S2.2.1 testosterone-stimulating peptides in males); no change to this listed for the 2027 List (in force 2027-01-01).
evidenceLevel: Approved, extensive use (for the labelled indications)

statusDetail.healthCanada: Previously approved; no marketed product found. Every clomiphene DIN found in the Drug Product Database is Cancelled Post Market: Clomid (Sanofi, DIN 02091879) 2020-07-15 (shortage database: discontinued 2015-11-25, business reasons); Serophene (EMD Serono, DIN 00893722) 2017-07-07; Serophene (Pharmascience, DIN 00640158) 2014-09-08; Clomid 50 mg (Merrell, DIN 00018031) 1996-09-09. A brand search for 'clomiphene' returned no generic products.
statusDetail.fda: Approved in the US: DailyMed lists current Clomid (Cosette, label revised 08/2023), Milophene and multiple generic clomiphene citrate tablet labels.

indications: Archived Canadian Clomid monograph: induction of ovulation in patients with persistent ovulatory dysfunction who desire pregnancy, only in patients who meet the listed evaluation criteria

Archived Canadian Serophene monograph: ovulatory failure in patients desiring pregnancy whose partners have adequate sperm and who have functional pituitary and ovarian systems with adequate endogenous estrogen
US label: treatment of ovulatory dysfunction in women desiring pregnancy
Use in men is not included in the Canadian monograph; it states there are no adequate or well-controlled studies showing effectiveness in male infertility
mechanism: Blocks estrogen feedback at the hypothalamus; the ovulatory response appears to be mediated by increased output of pituitary gonadotropins.

products.device: 50 mg white, round, flat-faced bevelled tablet, scored on one side

products.brand: Clomid 50 mg (Merrell Dow), cancelled post market

doseInfo.population: Women with ovulatory dysfunction (archived Canadian Clomid monograph, product no longer marketed)
doseInfo.regimen: First course 50 mg daily for 5 days, started at any time if there has been no recent uterine bleeding, or on or about day 5 of the cycle if bleeding occurs. If ovulation does not occur, a second course of 100 mg daily (two 50 mg tablets as a single daily dose) for 5 days, started as early as 30 days after the previous course
doseInfo.maxDose: 100 mg/day for 5 days (the monograph states dose or duration beyond this should never be undertaken)
doseInfo.durationOrContext: 3 courses constitute an adequate therapeutic trial; further treatment not recommended if no pregnancy after 3 ovulatory responses; long-term cyclic therapy not recommended beyond a total of about 6 cycles (including 3 ovulatory cycles)

doseInfo.population: Women with ovulatory dysfunction (US Clomid label)
doseInfo.regimen: Starts at 50 mg daily for 5 days
doseInfo.maxDose: Dose or duration beyond 100 mg/day for 5 days is not recommended
doseInfo.durationOrContext: Long-term cyclic therapy not recommended beyond a total of about six cycles

missedDose.text: Not stated in the fetched monograph or label text.

storage.unopened: Store in original container between 15 and 30 C; keep out of reach and sight of children

commonSideEffects: US label (trials, incidence above 1%): ovarian enlargement 13.6%, vasomotor flushes 10.4%, abdominal-pelvic discomfort/distention/bloating 5.5%, nausea and vomiting 2.2%, breast discomfort 2.1%, visual symptoms 1.5%
Canadian monograph: hot flashes and abdominal-pelvic discomfort are the more common side effects; ovarian enlargement and visual blurring also listed
warnings: Visual symptoms (blurring, spots or flashes): may be prolonged or irreversible, especially with higher dose or longer use; treatment is stopped and a complete eye examination done if any visual symptom occurs
Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), distinct from uncomplicated ovarian enlargement; abnormal ovarian enlargement is infrequent at recommended doses
Multiple pregnancy: the Canadian monograph states the rate has been increased up to tenfold when conception occurs in a treatment cycle
Prolonged use may increase the risk of borderline or invasive ovarian tumours
Hypertriglyceridemia, with or without pancreatitis, reported
Men: testicular tumours and gynecomastia reported in males using clomiphene (cause not established); male use is not a Canadian monograph indication
contraindications: Liver disease or history of liver dysfunction
Abnormal uterine bleeding of undetermined origin
Hypersensitivity or allergy to clomiphene or any ingredient
interactions: The archived Canadian Clomid monograph has no specific drug interaction section; its patient information says to disclose all medicines because clomiphene can affect how some other medicines work
specialPopulations: Breastfeeding: not known whether excreted in milk; may reduce lactation
Men: no adequate or well-controlled studies showing effectiveness in male infertility
wada: Clomifene is prohibited at all times (in and out of competition) as an anti-estrogenic substance (2026 Prohibited List, S4.2 Hormone and metabolic modulators); no change to this listed for the 2027 List.
evidenceLevel: Approved, extensive use (for the labelled indication); no longer marketed in Canada

statusDetail.healthCanada: Arimidex 1 mg tablet (DIN 02224135, AstraZeneca) marketed; original market date 1996-08-30. Generics: Apo-Anastrozole (DIN 02374420) marketed since 2012-10-25; a DPD brand search returns 30 anastrozole-named generic records (at least one, Teva-Anastrozole DIN 02313049, is Cancelled Post Market); status of the rest not individually checked.
statusDetail.fda: Not re-verified in this Canada-focused pass.

indications: Adjuvant treatment of postmenopausal women with hormone receptor positive early breast cancer
Hormonal treatment of advanced breast cancer in postmenopausal women
Use in men is not included in the Canadian monograph; its indications are limited to postmenopausal women, and it is not recommended in premenopausal women
mechanism: Potent, selective non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor; lowers serum estradiol without detectable effect on adrenal corticosteroid or aldosterone formation.

doseInfo.population: Postmenopausal women with breast cancer (adjuvant or advanced)
doseInfo.regimen: 1 mg orally once a day, ideally at the same time each day
doseInfo.maxDose: 1 mg once daily (the only listed dose)
doseInfo.durationOrContext: Adjuvant setting: treatment currently recommended for 5 years. No dose change for kidney impairment or mild-to-moderate liver impairment; not studied in severe liver impairment

missedDose.text: The monograph states a missed dose should be taken as soon as possible, as long as it is at least 12 hours before the next dose is due; it should not be taken within 12 hours of the next dose. (windowHours 12 is derived from the once-daily schedule minus the 12-hour rule.)

commonSideEffects: Common (1% to under 10%): bone pain, myalgia, carpal tunnel syndrome, vaginal dryness, hair thinning, rash, nausea, diarrhea, headache, raised liver enzymes
warnings: Serious warning: not recommended in premenopausal women; safety and efficacy not established
Bone: may reduce bone mineral density with possible increased fracture risk; osteoporosis risk is assessed and managed per local guidelines
Cholesterol: elevated serum cholesterol more common than with tamoxifen in ATAC (9% vs 3.5%); based on SABRE data no specific lipid monitoring is required
Heart: ischemic cardiovascular events reported more often than with tamoxifen (not statistically significant), mostly in patients with pre-existing ischemic heart disease
Depression: causal relation established in post-market data
Severe liver or kidney impairment: careful risk/benefit assessment
Use in men is not a Canadian monograph indication
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to anastrozole or any ingredient
interactions: Tamoxifen: should not be co-administered (no benefit from the combination in ATAC)
Estrogen-containing therapies, including estrogen-containing herbal products: should not be used, as they counteract estrogen suppression
Warfarin: no clinically relevant effect on warfarin pharmacokinetics or anticoagulant activity
CYP enzymes: clinically significant inhibition of other drugs' metabolism at 1 mg is unlikely
specialPopulations: Children: no pediatric indication authorized by Health Canada
Older adults: no differences in safety or effectiveness
Kidney: no dose change; liver: no change for mild-to-moderate, not studied in severe
wada: Aromatase inhibitors, including anastrozole, are prohibited at all times (in and out of competition) (2026 Prohibited List, S4.1 Hormone and metabolic modulators); no change to this listed for the 2027 List.
evidenceLevel: Approved, extensive use (for the labelled indications)
